title: Rehabilitation Robotics Market Size, Share & Forecast 2026-2032
executive_summary:
This is the thinnest evidence base of any market in this corpus, and the honest way to open a report on it is to say so. Published estimates put the 2025 base anywhere from $717 million to $5.13 billion -- a 7.15x spread -- and the published growth rates from 6.32% to 22.4%, with the house carrying the largest base publishing the smallest rate.

The category has three listed pure-plays that disclose revenue outright, which makes a published billion-dollar market immediately testable. Myomo reported $40.9 million for 2025. Lifeward, formerly ReWalk Robotics, reported about $22.0 million, down 14%. Ekso Bionics reported $12,799 thousand, down 29%. Together: $75.7 million -- 5.0% of the $1.51 billion Mordor Intelligence publishes for the same year, and 10.6% of the lowest published figure in the set.

The brief for a finding like this is to say what the other 95% would have to consist of, and the publisher's own segmentation answers it. Mordor states that stationary platforms are 65.3% of its 2025 market and upper-limb systems 54.6%. All three listed companies sell the opposite: wearable lower-limb exoskeletons, a wearable arm orthosis and an antigravity treadmill. The money, on the publisher's own account, is in stationary clinical gait and upper-limb therapy platforms sold into rehabilitation centres -- a tier owned by Hocoma, Motek, Tyromotion, Fourier Intelligence, Motorika, CYBERDYNE and Wandercraft, none of which is a US-listed pure-play and none of which we could find a revenue figure for. We name them and decline to size them.

One more fact belongs in any summary of this market. Ekso Bionics was merged into an AI infrastructure business called ChronoScale in May 2026, and the Ekso business unit was put up for sale on 1 October 2026. One of the three listed pure-plays ceased to be one during the first year of every forecast above. No published forecast mentions it.
market_context:
Rehabilitation robotics is two businesses that share a name and almost nothing else.

The first is a personal device, bought for an individual patient and reimbursed. CMS issued HCPCS code K1007 for the ReWalk personal exoskeleton effective 1 October 2020 -- the first such code for an exoskeleton -- and added exoskeletons to the Medicare brace benefit category on 1 January 2024, payable as a lump sum. The final amount, set in April 2024, was about $91,031 per device. That is an unusually transparent price for a medical device, and it makes the personal tier countable in a way almost nothing else in this corpus is.

The second is capital equipment: a stationary gait trainer or upper-limb therapy platform installed in a rehabilitation centre, costing six figures, bought on a hospital capital cycle and sold largely by private European, Japanese and Chinese manufacturers. On Mordor Intelligence's own figures this is where two thirds of the market sits.

The listed companies are all in the first business. The published market is mostly the second. That mismatch is the single most important thing to understand before quoting any figure in this category, and it explains why a sector whose entire public float discloses $75.7 million of revenue carries forecasts of $4 billion and more.
forecast_analysis:
The headline comes from Mordor Intelligence, read from the publisher's own page on 16 October 2026: $1.51 billion for 2025, $1.77 billion for 2026, $3.89 billion for 2031, a 17.10% CAGR for 2026-2031. The 2026 base is Mordor's own published figure. The 2032 endpoint continues its own rate one year past its own horizon (1.77 x 1.1710^6 = 4.56); interpolating forward lands 2031 on 3.90 against the published 3.89, and the implied rate between our endpoints is 17.09%.

It was chosen because it is the only source in the set we could read from the publisher's own page, the only one that states both what is in scope and what is out -- clinical and supervised care settings in, surgical robots and consumer fitness devices out -- and the only one that publishes the segment shares that make it possible to say where the market we cannot see is supposed to be.

That 17.10% should be read as a forecast about the undisclosed capital-equipment tier, not as a description of the visible industry. In 2025 Ekso Bionics shrank 29% and Lifeward shrank 14%; Myomo grew and guides 2026 to $45-47 million on a $40.9 million base. Lifeward's ReWalk Personal units rose 22% while that revenue line was flat at $8.5 million, which is volume growth with falling realised price -- the opposite of what a 17% revenue CAGR assumes. 360iResearch's $717 million for 2025, less than half Mordor's, is the low end of the published range, and it is the reading the disclosed record sits less awkwardly against.

market_overview.summary: On Mordor Intelligence's published series -- rehabilitation robots that assist, guide or measure patient movement in clinical and supervised care settings, excluding surgical robots and consumer fitness devices -- the market is $1.77 billion in 2026, projected to $4.56 billion by 2032 at a 17.10% CAGR. The lowest published estimate puts 2025 at $717 million against Mordor's $1.51 billion. All three listed pure-plays in the category sum to $75.7 million of 2025 revenue, 5.0% of Mordor's figure, so roughly 95% of this market is held by companies that disclose nothing. This report publishes the series and states that limitation rather than concealing it.

market_overview.adoption_level: Early; concentrated in specialist rehabilitation centres and a small reimbursed personal segment

drivers: A published Medicare lump-sum payment of about $91,031 per personal exoskeleton under HCPCS K1007, with exoskeletons inside the brace benefit category since 1 January 2024
Unit demand that is growing even where revenue is not: Lifeward's ReWalk Personal units rose 22% in 2025 and its Q4 sales rose 20%
Geriatric patients are 61.4% of the published market on Mordor's own segmentation, tying demand to a demographic trend that does not reverse
Therapist labour scarcity, which is the operational case for a platform that can deliver repetitions without one-to-one supervision
Wearable soft robots, which Mordor projects to grow at 29.6% to 2031, a lower-cost form factor than powered rigid exoskeletons
restraints: Two of the three listed pure-plays shrank in 2025 -- Ekso Bionics by 29% and Lifeward by 14% -- against published CAGRs of 16% to 22%
Capital budgets: two thirds of the market is stationary six-figure equipment bought on a hospital capital cycle, not a consumable
Balance-sheet fragility at the visible companies: Lifeward ended 2025 with $2.2 million of unrestricted cash and a $19.9 million net loss
Reimbursement outside the US personal exoskeleton code is largely undefined, so most of the world has no payment pathway for these devices
Flat revenue on rising units indicates price erosion in the one segment where a published price exists
opportunities: The undisclosed capital-equipment tier, where two thirds of the published revenue sits and where no listed pure-play currently competes at scale
Upper-limb therapy, 54.6% of the published market on Mordor's segmentation and the segment the listed exoskeleton companies barely address
Homecare, where a reimbursed personal device changes the delivery model rather than adding to a clinic's capital stock
Consolidation: the sale of the Ekso Bionics business unit announced on 1 October 2026 puts an established clinical and personal portfolio on the market
Distribution rather than manufacture, the route Ekso took in December 2025 by becoming exclusive US distributor of MediTouch's BalanceTutor system
challenges: Roughly 95% of the published market is held by companies that disclose no revenue, so no published figure in this category can be independently validated
The listed pure-plays are not representative of the market they are taken to represent: they sell wearables into a market that is two thirds stationary
The category is published under at least four mutually inconsistent names, from therapy rehabilitation robots at $926M by 2032 to robotic rehabilitation assistive technologies at $5.13B in 2025
Capital markets have begun exiting: one of three listed pure-plays was reverse-merged out of the industry inside the first forecast year

research_methodology.data_validation: Market size is taken from published third-party estimates, attributed by name, and presented as published estimates rather than verified measurements. Three grounding tests were run. First, the revenue of every listed pure-play in the category was summed -- Myomo $40.9M, Lifeward $22.0M and Ekso Bionics $12.8M, totalling $75.7M for 2025 -- and divided by each publisher's base-year total, giving 5.0% of Mordor's $1.51 billion and 10.6% of 360iResearch's $717 million. Second, because that leaves roughly 95% unaccounted for, the publisher's own segmentation was used to locate it: stationary platforms are stated at 65.30% of the 2025 market and upper-limb systems at 54.60%, while all three listed companies sell wearable or treadmill products, which places the remainder in a private, mostly non-US stationary capital-equipment tier that is named in this report and deliberately not sized. Third, the publisher's own exoskeleton segment share of 47.35% was applied to its 2025 total and divided by the CMS K1007 lump-sum amount of about $91,031, implying roughly 7,850 personal exoskeletons a year, against disclosed powered exoskeleton revenue of $21.3 million -- Lifeward's ReWalk Personal plus Ekso's whole company -- which is 2.98% of that segment and equivalent to about 234 devices. These tests do not establish that the published figures are wrong: an undisclosed tier cannot be measured, only named, and this report asserts no market size of its own. Ekso's figure is whole-company revenue including clinical devices and services rather than an exoskeleton-only line, and was read from a search summary of the 10-K; Lifeward's figures were read from third-party summaries because its own investor page returned HTTP 403; Myomo's FY2024 revenue was not obtained, so no 2025 growth rate for it is published; the K1007 amount was read from trade-press and company accounts rather than the CMS DMEPOS fee schedule, sources differ between $91,031 and $91,032, and the amount may have been revised since 2024; the exoskeleton segment also contains clinical systems priced well above the lump sum, so the implied unit count is an upper bound; and dividing company revenue by a third party's market total compares differently constructed numbers. No vendor market share is published because none is disclosed, and no regional or country split is published, because a single house's apportionment of a market that is 95% undisclosed is not a measurement.

faqs.question: How big is the rehabilitation robotics market?
faqs.answer: $1.77 billion in 2026 on Mordor Intelligence's published series, projected to $4.56 billion by 2032 at 17.10%. But published 2025 estimates range from $717 million to $5.13 billion, a 7.15x spread, and all three listed pure-plays in the category disclose only $75.7 million of revenue between them. This is the thinnest evidence base in our corpus and the report says so rather than concealing it.

faqs.question: Why is the published market 20 times the revenue of every listed company in it?
faqs.answer: Because the listed companies sell the wrong product. Mordor's own segmentation puts stationary platforms at 65.3% of the 2025 market and upper-limb systems at 54.6%, while Ekso and Lifeward sell wearable lower-limb exoskeletons, Myomo sells a wearable arm orthosis and AlterG is an antigravity treadmill. The money, on the publisher's own account, is in stationary clinical gait and upper-limb therapy platforms.

faqs.question: So who holds the other 95%?
faqs.answer: On the segmentation above it has to be the stationary clinical equipment tier: Hocoma and Motek (DIH Holding), Tyromotion, Motorika, Reha Technology, plus Fourier Intelligence, CYBERDYNE, Wandercraft and B-Temia. These are private, non-US-listed, or hold the business inside a larger group. We obtained no revenue figure for any of them, so we name them and decline to size them. That absence is the finding; filling it with an estimate would destroy it.

faqs.question: What does a personal exoskeleton cost?
faqs.answer: Medicare pays a lump sum under HCPCS code K1007, set in April 2024 at about $91,031 per device after a contractor initially proposed $94,617. Exoskeletons entered the brace benefit category on 1 January 2024. Applying that rate to Mordor's own exoskeleton segment implies roughly 7,850 devices a year, against disclosed powered exoskeleton revenue of $21.3 million -- about 234 devices. Clinical gait exoskeletons cost considerably more than the lump sum, so 7,850 is an upper bound.

faqs.question: Is the published 17% growth rate credible?
faqs.answer: It is a forecast about the undisclosed capital-equipment tier, not a description of the visible industry. In 2025 Ekso Bionics shrank 29% and Lifeward shrank 14%; Myomo grew and guides 2026 to $45-47 million on a $40.9 million base. Lifeward's ReWalk Personal units rose 22% while that revenue line was flat at $8.5 million, which is volume growth with price erosion -- the opposite of what a 17% revenue CAGR assumes.

faqs.question: What happened to Ekso Bionics?
faqs.answer: Applied Digital proposed in December 2025 to spin out its cloud business and combine it with Ekso Bionics to launch ChronoScale, an AI infrastructure company. The separation completed on 5 May 2026 and on 1 October 2026 ChronoScale announced the sale of the Ekso Bionics business unit. Ekso's former investor URL now redirects to ChronoScale's. One of the three listed pure-plays left the category during the first year of every forecast in the published literature, and none of those forecasts mentions it.

faqs.question: Why does this report show no regional breakdown?
faqs.answer: Mordor publishes a North America share of 39.60% for 2025, but that is one house's apportionment of a market roughly 95% of which is held by companies that disclose nothing, with no method stated. Publishing a regional table on that basis would give a precision the underlying evidence cannot support, so the section is omitted.

key_highlights: All three listed pure-plays sum to $75.7M of 2025 revenue -- 5.0% of the published market we adopt and 10.6% of the lowest published estimate
Published 2025 bases spread 7.15x ($717M to $5.13B) and published CAGRs 3.54x (6.32% to 22.4%)
Two thirds of the published market is stationary equipment (65.3% on the publisher's own figures) while every listed company sells wearables
Disclosed powered exoskeleton revenue of $21.3M is 2.98% of the publisher's own exoskeleton segment -- about 234 devices against an implied 7,850
Ekso Bionics shrank 29% in 2025, was merged into ChronoScale in May 2026, and the unit was put up for sale on 1 October 2026
Lifeward's ReWalk Personal units rose 22% while that revenue line stayed flat at $8.5M, and the company ended 2025 with $2.2M of unrestricted cash
CMS pays about $91,031 per personal exoskeleton under HCPCS K1007, one of the few published administered device prices anywhere in medtech
reader_takeaways: Treat any rehabilitation robotics market size as unvalidatable: roughly 95% of it sits with companies that disclose no revenue at all
Do not use the listed pure-plays as a proxy for this market -- they sell wearables into a market that is two thirds stationary capital equipment
If you are sizing the opportunity, size the stationary clinical platform tier, because that is where the published revenue is said to be
Model price erosion explicitly: the one segment with a published price shows units up 22% on flat revenue
Check the vintage of any forecast against the fact that one of three listed pure-plays exited the industry in 2026 -- none of the published forecasts has been revised for it
